p: Tiago taped HEARTH's floor plan onto the high bay concrete, with a red X for the hatch at one end.
Helen walked it and told them about a galley fire on the old station nine years ago, when the last crew member out had earplugs in and his door shut.
The team wrote each emergency from all four bunks, and quarter four, the far quarter half behind the hygiene wall, became everyone's worry.
Then Jun timed a depressurization run with Halo's crew trainers, and the hatch didn't close until a hundred and thirty three seconds.
The scenario allows a hundred and twenty, and quarter four is the last one out.
Jun Takeda. Junior engineer. He keeps the model and timed the walk.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He stood in quarter four and saw the problem.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He taped HEARTH out on the floor.
Odette. Safety engineer. She wants every scenario in seconds.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She still carries her fire note.
Amara Osei. Program manager, holding the schedule to the requirements review.
New in this chapter: Beto Salinas.
Somebody had written 133 on the whiteboard in the HEARTH room in red marker, and nobody erased it. By Monday of week five Wes had drawn a box around it. Nobody asked him why.

The number sat over everyone's head while Jun printed the first draft of the system requirements. It came to four hundred lines and nineteen pages, and he carried it to Nadia's desk with both hands like something that might spill.
It's everything, he said. Every stakeholder requirement, turned into what the module has to do. I didn't sleep much.

Nadia started reading at her desk and finished in the high bay, sitting on an equipment case at the edge of the blue tape, with a red pen she hadn't meant to uncap. Some of it was very good. Line forty one said the cabin shall be quiet. Line ninety tried to do the whole hatch in one sentence. Line two hundred and six said the module shall be safe.
She could hear Colleen already. You can't fly a line that says be safe.

The system requirements review was at the end of week six. After that, these four hundred lines would be the baseline, the thing every drawing, every test and every argument for the next two and a half years would point back to. She uncapped the pen the rest of the way.
Colleen's Flight Notes: write it so it can be checked.
From what they need to what it must do.

Colleen came in Thursday for the advisory board and stayed after, in the chair next to Nadia's desk, with her own red pen and Jun's draft between them. She'd read the whole thing the night before and circled the good lines too, which Nadia hadn't expected.
System requirements definition starts from the stakeholder requirements, which are written from the user's side.

Here's the card for system requirements definition. Its purpose is to turn the users' view into a technical view of what the system must do, how well, and under what limits, without designing it. It takes in the stakeholder requirements, the operational concept and its scenarios, the MOEs, constraints such as volume and launch mass, and what's known about the interfaces. It puts out the system requirements, a verification method for each, the measures of performance that matter most, traces up and down, and, once the system requirements review approves them, the requirements baseline. Architecture definition takes the requirements next. Design and verification work from them too, and configuration management takes custody of the baseline.

System requirements come in a few kinds. A functional requirement says what the system must do: detect smoke, sound the alarm. A performance requirement says how well: within so many seconds, at so many decibels. An interface requirement says what must cross a boundary and in what form. A constraint limits the choices without being a function, like the launch mass, a standard the program must meet, or a material nobody may use. Many requirements also carry a quality characteristic, such as reliability or maintainability, that shapes the whole design. Most good requirements pair a function with its performance, in a plain pattern: the subject, then shall, then what it does, how well, and under what conditions. A function with no number can't be verified. A number with no function has nothing to hang on.
A requirement is a promise you can check, Colleen said. If you can't check it, it's a wish.
How the exam asks it. Stakeholder requirements are the user's view. System requirements are the system's view. System requirements get verified, and they're the main input to architecture definition.
She drew a line through "the cabin shall be quiet." A checklist item that says check the engine is useless, she said. Oil pressure in the green arc, I can do in the dark.

A good requirement is necessary: something real breaks or goes missing without it. It's appropriate: written at the right level for this system, saying what, not how. It's unambiguous: only one reasonable reading. It's complete: it stands on its own without another document to explain it. It's singular: one requirement, one thing, so it can pass or fail on its own. It's feasible: it can be met within cost, schedule, technology and physics. It's verifiable: there's a way to show it was met. It's correct: it says what the need actually is. And it's conforming: it follows the project's agreed pattern and style. Traceability isn't on that list. It's an attribute every requirement carries, a link up to its parent and source, and it comes up again later as a method. The whole set should be complete and consistent too, with no gaps and no two requirements fighting each other. Jun's draft broke most of these somewhere, which is normal for a first draft. The point of a shared list is that a review argues about the module, not about taste.

Each requirement also carries attributes, the information that travels with it: an identifier, the rationale for why it exists, its source and parent, its owner, its priority, its verification method and its status. Rationale is the one people skip and later miss the most. It tells the next engineer what the number protects, so they can see what a change would cost. The set has characteristics of its own as well. Beyond complete and consistent, it should be feasible as a whole, understandable to the people who'll use it, and able to be validated against the needs. A set that covers normal operation and says nothing about startup, shutdown, failure or maintenance isn't complete, however good each line is.

Derived requirements are ones the stakeholders never asked for but the design needs: a connector type, a heat limit on a box, a time budget for one step of an alarm. They come from architecture choices, decisions and analysis, and each one traces up to whatever caused it, so it can be questioned when that parent changes. After the baseline, requirements still move. A few changes are normal. A steady stream of them, called volatility or churn, is a leading indicator that the needs weren't understood or that the scope is creeping, and it earns a measure of its own.

Line 41 of the system requirements, before and after. Before, the cabin shall be quiet. After, as S R 41: with all HEARTH systems in their nominal sleep period mode, the continuous noise level at the head position of each sleep station shall not exceed 45 decibels, A weighted. Its parent is S T K 12, crew sleep, and it's verified by test.

How the exam asks it. Words like quick, easy, adequate, reliable, user friendly and safe, with no number or condition, are the exam's favorite signs of an unverifiable or ambiguous requirement. Two "shalls" or an "and" joining two behaviors means it isn't singular.

Every requirement gets a verification method when it's written, not when the test campaign starts. There are four main ones. Inspection is looking: the label is there, the part number matches, the dimension is right. Analysis is calculation, modeling and simulation, for things you can't fully test, like fifteen years of micrometeoroids. Demonstration is operating the system and watching that it does the thing, without instrumented measurements: a crew member opens the hatch without tools. Test is operating it under controlled conditions and measuring: the leak rate at pressure, the noise at the pillow. You'll also see analogy or similarity, using evidence from an item already verified under the same conditions, but the four carry almost every program.

Picking the method is part of writing the requirement. Ask what evidence would convince a skeptical reviewer, at what cost, and at what level of the system. A requirement nobody can verify by any method has to be rewritten until somebody can. And the method chosen now becomes a line in the verification plan, with the test equipment and facilities it needs planned well ahead.
Test is the one testers love, Colleen said, not looking up. It's also the most expensive. Pick the one that gives you real evidence for that requirement, and nothing fancier.

How the exam asks it. Match the method to the evidence. Present or marked: inspection. Can't be tested in full: analysis. Observed operation, pass or fail: demonstration. Measured result under controlled conditions: test.

Traceability is a method, not a spreadsheet. Each system requirement links up to the stakeholder requirement or analysis it came from, and down to its verification and the parts of the design that meet it. Done in both directions, it tells you when a requirement has no parent, an orphan that may not be necessary, and when a need has no requirement under it, a gap. It's also how you find everything a change will touch. Jun's model can hold those links, which is the start of a digital thread through the program.

In a model, those links have names. A lower requirement is derived from its parent. A design element satisfies a requirement. A test case verifies it. A more detailed statement refines it. A requirement diagram can show all four at once, and a trace report built from them answers the review board's favorite question: how do you know every requirement was verified?

At the system requirements review, the set becomes the requirements baseline. From then on configuration management controls it: a change needs a change request, an impact assessment, and a decision by the board that owns the baseline. Open values marked to be determined are allowed in a baseline, if each one has an owner and a date. A value that's written in but still needs confirming is marked to be resolved, with the same owner and date.

Configuration management starts with a plan for what it will control and who decides changes, then does five standing jobs. Identification names the items under control and the baseline each belongs to. Change control runs every proposed change through a request, an impact assessment and a decision by the board. Status accounting keeps the record of each item's approved version and where every change stands. Audits, which the standard calls configuration evaluation, check that the product and its documents match each other and the baseline. Release control decides which version is issued for use and when, so nobody builds from a drawing that wasn't approved.

Here's the card for configuration management. Its purpose is to manage and control the system's elements and configurations over the whole life cycle, and to keep the product and its records consistent with each other. It takes in the items chosen for control, the baselines, and every request to change them. It puts out the configuration management plan, the controlled baselines, the board's decision on each change, status accounting records, audit findings and released items. Everyone who designs, builds, tests or ships works to those next.

Programs usually name three baselines. The functional baseline holds the approved system level requirements, and the requirements baseline set at this review is that kind. The allocated baseline holds the requirements given to each element, usually set around preliminary design. The product baseline holds the approved build to design, usually set at critical design. Each one is a fixed point the next stage is measured against, and a change to any of them goes through the board. When a part has already been built a little wrong and the team wants to use it as it is, without changing the design, that's a request for a waiver, decided by the same board for that part alone.
Information management is the wider job: getting the right information to the right people, current, protected and with the right access, and keeping the record of it.

Here's the card for information management. Its purpose is to get the right information to the right people, complete, current, valid and protected, for as long as it's needed. It takes in the information the project creates and receives, along with the rules that apply to it, such as the agreement's data terms, export control and privacy. It puts out the information management strategy, the information items themselves in agreed forms where people can find them, the access rules, and the records of what was stored, changed, archived or disposed of. Every process uses that information next, and configuration management controls the items that are baselined.

The work has two halves. Preparing means deciding up front what information the project will create and use, in what formats, who may see each kind, and how long it's kept. Performing means collecting it, storing it, protecting it, getting it to people, archiving it, and finally disposing of it on schedule. Test data that lives on one person's laptop, or a lab file format nobody's tools can open, is an information management failure that started in the planning. The verification method written beside each requirement is information too. It becomes a line in the verification plan, and the verification process runs that plan later.

Colleen tapped the margin where Nadia had written Wes's name twice. Watch the requirements nobody writes down, she said. Wes has thirty years of rules in his head. Every one of them is probably right, and none of them is in your baseline. An organization that keeps its best knowledge in one man's head loses it the day he retires.

Rules like Wes's have a name. The handbook keeps a set of systems engineering heuristics, rules of thumb drawn from experience, such as keep it simple, or expect the trouble at the interfaces. A heuristic guides judgment where the principles and processes leave room. It isn't claimed to hold for every system, the way a principle is, so it gets checked against the case in front of you. Written down, it can be checked and shared.
Getting that kind of knowledge out of people and into a form the next program can use is the job of knowledge management, and it'll come up again.

How the exam asks it. Orphan requirements may not be necessary. Needs with no requirements under them are gaps. After the baseline, every change goes through change control with an impact assessment. Know the configuration management activities: planning, then identification, change control, status accounting, audit and release control. Functional, allocated and product baselines usually set at requirements, preliminary design and critical design. A built part used as is needs a waiver. A heuristic is a rule of thumb from experience, not a principle that always holds.
Tuesday Nadia sat down with Jun and the red-marked draft. He looked at the ink and then at her.
Most of the lines traced to a scenario on the tape. Some of the language, though, would never survive a test engineer.
How bad is it? he asked, and waited with his pen capped. What does Nadia do with the draft?
A. Walk ten lines with Jun against the characteristics, then let him finish.
B. Rewrite the forty worst lines herself tonight and hand Jun a clean draft.
C. Send the draft to Halo's reviewers this week and collect their comments.
D. Accept the draft for now and tighten the wording later, during design.

They take ten lines together at the edge of the tape, slowly. Is it necessary, is there one reading, can it be checked, is it one thing, can it be built, where did it come from. Line two hundred and six, the module shall be safe, takes twenty minutes on its own, because Jun defends it the whole way. Everybody knows what safe means. Tell me how Tiago tests it. He opens his mouth and closes it. Then he takes the pen from her and splits the line into four himself, one for each hazard they'd walked on the tape with Helen. By the twentieth line he's finding the problems before she does, and around the thirtieth he finds one in a line she'd marked good.
That's the one. The requirement characteristics are a shared standard the whole team can apply. Reviewing against them, and teaching them, fixes the set and the people who'll keep writing it.
Line ninety was the hatch. "The hatch shall open within 10 seconds and seal to the leak limit and be operable by one crew member from either side."
It's all about the hatch, Jun said. Isn't it cleaner in one place?
Jun's happy with line ninety as it stands. What should Nadia do with it?
A. Keep it as one line, with a margin note that it covers three things.
B. Keep line ninety as written, a single requirement for a single component.
C. Move the details into the hatch spec and keep "the hatch shall work properly."
D. Split line ninety into three requirements, one for each hatch behavior.

Nadia has him split it into one requirement for each thing the hatch does. Three lines, three parents, three verification methods: test for the opening time, test for the leak rate, demonstration for one person operation. Jun renumbers them and looks pleased about it.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Singular means one requirement states one thing. It costs a few lines and gets you clean verification, clean traceability, and changes that touch only what they should.
Decision three. Where did this come from.
Wes wanted the requirements in a spreadsheet, the way FRO had always kept them, one tab per subsystem. Jun wanted them in the model, linked to the stakeholder needs and the scenarios.
I can read a spreadsheet, Wes said. Everybody can read a spreadsheet.
Wes wants a spreadsheet per subsystem, and Jun wants every line linked to its source. Where should traceability live?
A. Keep Wes's spreadsheet and add a column for each line's parent requirement.
B. Trace each requirement down to its verification and skip the upward links.
C. Keep the links in the model and generate a spreadsheet view for Wes.
D. Use Wes's spreadsheet now and add traceability once the set settles.

Nadia keeps the links in Jun's model and has it print a spreadsheet view for Wes. Jun runs the first trace report that afternoon. Twelve requirements have no parent. Four needs have no requirement under them at all. Wes reads the spreadsheet view and says it looks like a spreadsheet, which is as close to approval as he gets.

Exactly right. Traceability is a method: links up to the source and down to verification, kept in both directions, so you can find orphans, gaps, and the reach of a change. A model holds the links. A view gives everyone access.
Decision four. Quiet enough to sleep.

Line forty one, the cabin shall be quiet, came from a stakeholder requirement about crew sleep. Helen's notes said the old station was so loud that some crews slept with earplugs every night, and under that, underlined: if it's quiet, they don't need earplugs, and they hear the alarm.
Tiago read it over Nadia's shoulder. How do I test quiet?
Line forty one says only that the cabin shall be quiet. What should Nadia do with it?
A. Reword it as "as quiet as practical" to leave room for trades.
B. Set a noise limit in dBA at each bunk's head position in sleep mode.
C. Drop the line and leave noise to the air system's design rules.
D. Ask Helen to define quiet and record her answer under the requirement.
They set forty five decibels, A weighted, at the head of each sleep station, with the module in its sleep mode, and trace it to crew sleep. Tiago nods. That I can put a microphone on.
That's the one. A verifiable requirement says what's measured, where, under what conditions, and to what limit. Now there's one reading and one way to prove it.
Decision five. Three things to open it.
Odette came to Wednesday's requirements meeting with a hazard list and one page of proposed safety requirements. The first hazard was the hatch opening by accident while the module was pressurized.
That one's catastrophic, she said. So. What has to break for that hatch to open with air behind it?
Odette's first hazard is the hatch coming open by accident on a pressurized module. What should the requirement say?
A. Require three independent inhibits against opening under pressure.
B. Write that the hatch shall not open inadvertently and leave controls to design.
C. Hold the safety requirements until the hazard analysis is done after PDR.
D. Take Odette's page as written for the hatch safety requirements.

The requirement Nadia writes calls for three independent inhibits against the hatch opening under pressure. Jun links it to the hazard and gives it a verification method. Odette reads the wording, changes one word, and initials it.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Safety requirements come from hazard analysis and control specific hazards. For a catastrophic hazard on a crewed system, that means fault tolerance stated in the requirement, traced to the hazard report it closes.
Helen's comments came back Thursday. On the egress requirement she'd crossed out the value and written 60 seconds, and under it, smaller: that's as long as I can watch the clock.
Jun pulled up the tape times. It took forty five seconds just to wake up and get out of a bunk.
Helen crossed out the egress value and wrote sixty seconds. What should Nadia do?
A. Mark the value to be determined until the layout is drawn and measured.
B. Write 60 seconds as Helen asked, as a hard target for the design.
C. Walk Helen through the wake times and agree a value some layout can meet.
D. Write 60 seconds as a goal and the reference leak time as the requirement.

Nadia calls Helen and walks her through the wake times, bunk by bunk. Helen looks at them for a long minute. I know, she says. I wanted to see it in writing that I can't have it. They settle on the time Halo's reference leak allows, with the rationale written under it. The current layout doesn't meet it, but some layout can, and that's the design's problem to solve.
Exactly right. Feasible means it can be achieved within physics, technology, cost and schedule, by some design. Use the data to agree a value, and keep the rationale with the requirement.

Saturday she met Beto Salinas for coffee in Castle Rock, which Beto called halfway and wasn't. He'd been her bench partner at the avionics shop in Colorado Springs, and he was still there. He brought her the shop's news like a care package: the new hire on her old bench had already cooked two power supplies, the cold chamber door still stuck in the mornings, and somebody had finally thrown out her chair. It squeaked, he said. Nobody could run a test without thinking about you. He took her laptop without asking, scrolled to the verification column, and laughed out loud.

Test. Test. Test. Test, he read. You still love a green PASS, Brooks. He knew why. He'd never once asked her about it, which was one of the reasons they were still friends. Same job, different hardware, he said, and pushed the laptop back across the table. So do it the way you used to.
Beto laughs at a verification column that says test on every line. How should Nadia set the methods?
A. Leave the methods blank for Tiago to fill in with his test plan.
B. Go line by line and pick the method that gives real evidence for each.
C. Move most lines to analysis and keep test for the safety items.
D. Keep test on every line, the strongest evidence for a crewed module.

They do sixty lines over two refills. Labels go to inspection, the hatch handle to demonstration, leak rate to test, and fifteen years of debris to analysis. Beto steals the last of her muffin as his fee.

That's the one. Each requirement gets the verification method that actually produces the evidence it needs: inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test. Assigning methods as you write the requirement keeps the requirement verifiable.
Decision eight. Fifteen years of gravel.
One requirement made Tiago put his coffee down. The shielding had to keep the probability of a penetrating micrometeoroid or debris strike below a set value over fifteen years in orbit.
Then he picked it back up and grinned. There's a light gas gun in Ohio. It shoots panels, not years. The question was what to call the rest of the proof.
The shielding requirement holds for fifteen years in orbit. Which verification approach fits it?
A. Inspect the shield's certificates, thickness and drawing at delivery.
B. Use analysis with the debris model, anchored by impact tests on panels.
C. Rewrite the requirement as a shield thickness the shop can measure.
D. Test a full shield section at the impact lab and treat it as the proof.

The rest is analysis, Nadia says, with the debris model checked against real shots. Tiago books the gas gun for a dozen sample panels. The shots calibrate the model, and the model covers fifteen years. I can stand behind that, he says.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. When the full condition can't be tested, analysis is the method, and tests on samples give it real data to stand on. Most hard requirements are verified by a combination like this.
Decision nine. Everyone wants the keys.

Halo's program office called Monday of week six. They wanted edit access to FRO's requirements in the model before the review, so their engineers could fix wording directly instead of sending comments.
It would save a week of email, Amara said. Your call.
Halo's program office wants to fix wording in FRO's model directly. What access should Halo get?
A. Email Halo a weekly PDF and collect their comments in a spreadsheet.
B. Keep Halo out of the set until it's baselined at the review.
C. Give Halo read access to the live set with a comment tool on each line.
D. Give Halo edit access to the requirements in the model before the review.

Nadia gives Halo read access to the live set and a comment box on every line, but not the pen. Halo sees the current set every day and comments on the line itself. FRO's people make the edits, and every one has a name and a reason. Halo's lead engineer says it's better than what they asked for.
Exactly right. Information management gives each stakeholder the right access to current information, and keeps changes controlled and recorded. Write the rule down so it holds after this week.

The set froze for review on Tuesday of week six. On Wednesday Wes dropped a sticky note on Nadia's keyboard with three lines in his square capitals. Hatch handle on both sides, one hand, no tools. Seat track down both sides of the aisle for stowage. All harnesses in the overhead channel.
Obvious stuff, he said. Every cargo module had them. Just put them in.

She read them twice. They were good rules. She could almost see where each one had come from: somebody who'd once needed a tool to open a hatch, somebody with nowhere to clip a bag, somebody chasing a rubbed through wire under a floor panel.

Every one of those cost somebody a bad week, he said. I'm saving you the week. He was already turning to go. The review was Thursday, and through the glass Amara was walking the review package down the hall in a box.
The set froze for review Tuesday, and Wes has three lines he wants added. What should Nadia do?
A. Tell Wes the set is frozen and leave the three lines out.
B. Add the three lines to the frozen set before Thursday's review.
C. List them in the review package as open issues for the reviewers.
D. Write each one up as a change request with Wes's rationale.

Nadia writes each of his lines up as a change request, leaves the reason blank, and carries the three forms to his desk herself. Wes looks at them and then at her. Paperwork. Your reasons are better than mine would be, she says, and stays standing there. He sighs and uncaps a pen. The hatch handle gets two lines: a station crew in gloves who couldn't open a cargo hatch without a tool, and the forty minutes it took to find one. The harness channel gets two more: a wire rubbed through under a floor panel on the fourth cargo module, and the week it took to find it. Then he gets to the seat track and stops. It's a seat track, he says. Every module has one. I'm not writing an essay for a rail. He hands her the three with one box empty. The requests go into the queue with numbers anyway, and the empty box goes in with them.
That's the one. Configuration management controls changes to a baselined or frozen set. A change request captures the proposal and the reason, so it can be assessed and decided, not slipped in.
Amara set up the first configuration control board for Friday after the review. Wes's three change requests were the first items on it. She asked Nadia what the board would need to decide.
Wes, passing, said the board would need about thirty seconds.
Amara's first configuration control board meets Friday. What should Nadia bring it?
A. Approval of all three now, with the impact work done during design.
B. Each item's cost and schedule impact, for Amara to weigh against budget.
C. Wes's own recommendation on each of the three design rules he wrote.
D. An impact trace of each change across everything linked to it.

Nadia wants the board to see everything each change touches, so Jun runs the trace. The hatch handle maps cleanly to a need. The seat track narrows the aisle by eleven centimeters, and the egress model gets slower. The overhead harness touches two interfaces nobody has defined yet. The board has something real to decide.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Impact assessment uses traceability to find everything a change touches: other requirements, interfaces, performance, cost, schedule and verification. Then the board decides with eyes open.
Decision twelve. What goes in the baseline.
Wednesday night Jun's trace report came to three hundred and ninety six requirements. Eleven still had values marked to be determined, including the egress layout's test conditions.
Wes wanted the review pushed until the open values were closed. Amara wanted to baseline it and stop talking about it.
Jun's trace report shows eleven requirements still marked to be determined. What should happen at the review?
A. Baseline it with an owner and a closure date on every open TBD.
B. Pull the eleven open requirements and add them back by change request.
C. Push the review back until every one of the eleven TBDs is closed.
D. Baseline it as is and let design resolve the open TBDs as it goes.

Nadia sides with neither. They baseline it, with an owner and a closing date on every open value. The review package lists all eleven on one page: who, by when, and from what analysis. The reviewers ask about three of them, and all three have answers.
Exactly right. The requirements baseline is set at the review and controlled after it. Open values are acceptable when each is tracked with an owner and a closure plan, so the baseline stays honest.
The night before the review Nadia was still at her desk at nine when her phone lit up.
A text from Dad. BIG DAY TOMORROW. ROSIE DREW YOU A NEW ROCKET. 5 IN THE WINDOW NOW. SHE PUT YOU IN. CALLIE SAYS YOU MISSED SUNDAY. SHE WONT SAY IT SO IM SAYING IT.

She read it at her desk with the review package open on the other screen. She typed an apology and deleted it. What she sent was shorter: she'd call Callie Sunday, and Rosie should save her the window seat. Then she put Sunday at noon in her calendar with an alarm on it, and sat there a minute with nothing to check.

The review ran all of Thursday in the big conference room. Helen was on the screen from Halo, and an observer from OCSC, the federal office that audits human rating, sat in the back writing in a notebook nobody got to see. Jun presented the trace. Tiago presented the verification methods. Odette walked through the hazard controls without once raising her voice.

Halfway through the morning a man from Halo's program office, on the screen beside Helen, asked to go back to line forty one. He'd read ahead. The noise line couldn't be proved until the real air rack was running in the module, he said, and that was more than a year out. Could FRO carry it as a goal, and keep the hard requirements for air and pressure?

Helen unmuted before anyone at the table could answer. She read the line out loud, all of it: forty five decibels, A weighted, at the head of each sleep station, in sleep mode. Then she read the parent under it. That's not comfort, she said. That's the man with his earplugs in. At forty five, he leaves them out, and then he hears the alarm.

The chair looked down the table at FRO. Amara, beside Nadia, had already written the words integrated noise test on her pad and underlined them once, which meant money. A goal would cost nothing until the day somebody slept in the module.

It stays a requirement, Nadia said. Tiago proves it on the whole module with the rack running. If the rack can't meet forty five, I'd rather find out a year early than the night the crew moves in. The man from Halo said that was FRO's test and FRO's money. It's our test, she said. Amara didn't cross anything out.
At lunch the observer from OCSC found Nadia by the coffee. She was older than anyone else in the room, with a federal badge clipped upside down on her lanyard. Your egress line. Who's it for?
Nadia thought about the tape, and the square half behind the hygiene wall. Whoever's in quarter four.
The observer wrote one line in the notebook and closed it.

At four the chair read the result: proceed, with four action items. The requirements baseline was set. Helen said, on the screen, that it was the first requirements set she'd read that sounded like it had met a crew. Amara shook Nadia's hand in the hallway and didn't say anything about the schedule, which was new.

Wes's three change requests sat in the board's queue for Friday, numbered. Two had his rationale in his square capitals. The seat track's box was still empty. All three were outside the baseline, where they belonged until somebody decided.
Friday morning Nadia went to the structures area to borrow the latest hatch drawing. It was on Wes's plotter, still warm, revision C. She read the notes block out of habit.

Notes seven, eight and nine on revision C of the hatch and aisle drawing. Hatch handle on both sides, one hand, no tools. Seat track on both sides of the aisle, full length. All harness routed in the overhead channel. Drawn by W. Harland, Monday of week six.
Three notes, drawn into the structure before anybody had decided them. The aisle on the drawing was already eleven centimeters narrower than the aisle on the tape.
The baseline was fourteen hours old. Wes's drawing was three days older.
The board met at ten to decide whether Wes could have what he'd already drawn. Nadia rolled the sheet under her arm and walked it over to him first.
